694.title: Sulayman's du'a
694.hook: inspire me to be grateful, and to do good that pleases You (27:19)
694.howItsDone: Some Muslims say the du'a of 27:19, rabbi awzi'ni an ashkura ni'mataka, in moments of success or gratitude; the similar words of 46:15 are also taught as a du'a for parents and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zakariyya's du'a, and your line, don't leave me alone. Today, a king with everything, stopped in his tracks by an ant.

An army on the march: people, jinn and birds, the Qur'an says, all in their ranks, and at the front a king, Sulayman, the one the Bible calls Solomon. They come to a valley full of ants. And one ant calls out to the others: get into your homes, or Sulayman and his soldiers will crush you without even noticing. Surah twenty-seven says Sulayman heard her. He had been taught the speech of birds, and here he understands an ant. The king at the head of that army stops, and smiles.
screen: `AN ARMY IN THE VALLEY OF THE ANTS.`

segments.voice: What he does next is surah twenty-seven, verse nineteen. He smiled, laughing at her words, and prayed. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord, arouse me to be thankful for Thy favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents, and to do good that shall be pleasing unto Thee." The word Pickthall renders arouse me is awzi'ni. Translators give it as inspire me, keep me devoted, or urge me on. Either way, Sulayman doesn't trust himself to stay grateful on his own. He asks to be kept at it. Count what he has: a kingdom, an army, the speech of birds. And the moment that gift shows him a tiny creature worried about her family, his first reaction isn't pride. It's thanks, and a request for help to keep thanking. Notice who he includes: me and my parents. The gift that let him hear an ant didn't start with him. Later in the same surah, when a throne is brought to him in the blink of an eye, he says, in effect, this is from my Lord's bounty, to test me whether I give thanks or turn ungrateful. So for Sulayman, a skill is also a question. One more detail: nearly the same words come back in surah forty-six, from an ordinary person who reaches forty years old. The king's prayer turns out to be a prayer for anyone who has been given anything.
screen: `AWZI'NI: KEEP ME AT IT, INSPIRE ME.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you can do, cook a dish without a recipe, calm a crying baby, fix a sink, make a stranger laugh, and trace it back to who taught you or gave you the time to learn it. If you pray, thank Allah for the skill and the people behind it, in your own words or with Sulayman's; if you don't, simply hold the skill and the people with it, gratefully.
Sulayman's du'a. A king who heard an ant, smiled, and asked to be kept grateful, for himself and for his parents, and to do good that pleases Allah. Today's word.
Your line: inspire me to be grateful. A gift is also a question. That's day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: The believers' du'a
695.hook: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve, and give us mercy from You (3:8)
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book read through
695.howItsDone: Some Muslims say 3:8, rabbana la tuzigh qulubana, after the daily prayers or in personal du'a, alongside the Prophet's own prayer, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sulayman and the ant, and your line, inspire me to be grateful. Today, the last du'a of this run, spoken not by a prophet but by a whole group of believers.

Umm Salamah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, noticed something. A prayer he said more than any other, she reported, was this: O turner of hearts, keep my heart firm on Your religion. She asked him why that one, so often. He answered, in the hadith recorded by at-Tirmidhi, that every human heart lies between two of the fingers of Allah, and He turns it as He wills. The Prophet himself, asking again and again for his own heart to be kept.

The Qur'an puts a request very like it in the mouths of a whole group. Surah three, verse seven, talks about the book itself: some verses are clear and plain, others open to more than one reading. Some people chase the unclear ones to stir up trouble, it says. But those firmly grounded in knowledge say: we believe in it, it is all from our Lord. Then verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us, and bestow upon us mercy from Thy Presence. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Bestower." Look who is praying. Not beginners. The people the verse calls firm in knowledge, who have studied the hard parts. And look at after Thou hast guided us. This isn't a prayer to find the way. It's a prayer not to lose it. Guidance, in this verse, isn't a trophy on a shelf. It can slip. The Prophet's own words make the fit audible: muqallib al-qulub, turner of hearts. Qalb, heart, and the verb to turn share their letters, as if a heart is the thing that turns. So those who know the hard parts ask, as the Prophet did, to be kept. This week has been prophets' du'as: Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Sulayman. Today's belongs to everyone who has been guided at all.
screen: `THE FIRMLY GROUNDED SAY: ALL FROM OUR LORD.`
`DON'T LET OUR HEARTS STRAY, AFTER GUIDANCE.`

segments.voice: Find your heartbeat if you can, steady without your help. If you pray, say the believers' words, in Arabic if you know them or in English: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You have guided us, and give us mercy from You; some Muslims say it after the daily prayer. If you don't, hold one thing you'd hate to drift from while the heart keeps time.
Qalb: heart. It shares its letters with the verb to turn, as if a heart is the very thing that turns, the word behind the Prophet's own prayer to be kept steady. Today's word.
Your line: keep my heart. Even the firmly grounded ask to be kept. Until tomorrow.

696.title: Year two close: the book read through
696.hook: from the Opening to the thirtieth part, the whole Qur'an has now been heard once
696.howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a reading of the whole Qur'an, a khatm, especially during Ramadan, often closing with a gathering and du'a, and in many communities a new reading begins at once with the Fatiha and the opening of al-Baqarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qalb, the heart, the thing that turns, and your line, keep my heart. Today, the last day of year two, and a whole book behind you.

On the first day of this year, your line was: from the opening, onward. Since then this path has walked from surah one, the Fatiha, through the Cow and the Family of Imran, past Yusuf and Maryam and the Cave, through the Ant and the Stories, all the way to surah seventy-seven. Year one had already carried the last part, the thirtieth, from seventy-eight to the end. Put the two years together, and something has happened quietly.

Every one of the hundred and fourteen surahs has now been heard on this path at least once. The short surahs came whole. The long ones came by theme, a passage and an idea at a time, not every verse read aloud. So this is a first hearing, not a full recitation. But it has a shape Muslims know well. Finishing the Qur'an from beginning to end is called a khatm, a sealing or completing, and it has a long history. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the angel Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. Many Muslims aim for a khatm each Ramadan; some families and mosques gather to hear its final surahs together and make du'a. In many communities, the moment one reading ends, the next begins: back to the Fatiha, and the first lines of the Cow. The book has no last page, only a place where you turn around. The year was built in five blocks: the Opening and the long Medinan surahs; prophets, parables and light; a holy-days interlude; the middle of the book; and the run toward the thirtieth part. The last month gathered it all: the prophets named, the women remembered, justice, mercy, the earth, and this past week, the prophets' own du'as. Pickthall's translation of the Fatiha opens: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." That is where the reading began. It is also where the next one starts.
screen: `A FIRST HEARING, NOT A FULL RECITATION.`

segments.voice: If you pray, recite the Fatiha, in Arabic if you know it, or hear its meaning in English, line by line. Then bring back one verse from this year that stayed with you, maybe a healing and a mercy, maybe I was wrong, maybe no compulsion, and say it once or simply hold it. If you don't pray, let one line from the year come back, and notice why that one stayed.
Khatm. A sealing, a completing: every surah of the Qur'an now heard once on this path, and a door back to the Fatiha. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, heard once. Tomorrow, year three: the people who carried this book. Year two, done.

697.title: The long story
697.hook: a year of people: the Prophet ﷺ, those who walked beside him, and those who came after
697.howItsDone: Sirah books and mosque classes teach the life of the Prophet ﷺ alongside the Qur'an, and Muslims pray, in words from surah fifty-nine, for forgiveness for those who came before them in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two with a khatm. Your line was: the whole book, heard once.

A book doesn't walk from one century to the next on its own. Someone memorized it. Someone recited it at dawn to a half-asleep child. Someone copied it, taught it, argued over it, carried it on a camel or in a coat pocket. For two years this path has listened to the Qur'an itself, surah by surah. This year turns to the people standing next to it: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the ones who walked beside him, and the long line who came after. Today's word is the shape of that year.
screen: `A BOOK DOESN'T WALK ON ITS OWN.` → `TWO YEARS OF THE TEXT.` → `NOW, THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Muslims have a word for the story of the Prophet's life: sirah. One of the early lives that comes down to us was put together by Ibn Ishaq, and it reaches us largely through a later editor, Ibn Hisham. Then there are the companions, the sahabah. The Qur'an remembers one of them without giving his name. In surah nine it describes the Prophet hiding in a cave on his escape from Mecca, and Pickthall's translation reads: "the second of two; when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." Commentators identify that comrade as Abu Bakr. A whole friendship, inside one verse. Then the ones after. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet is reported to say that the best people are his own generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them. A hadith comes with its isnad, the chain of names attached to it: this one heard it from that one, who heard it from another. Every saying arrives holding someone's hand. So here is this year's rule. The Qur'an and the major hadith collections come first. The sirah adds color and detail, and where a story is told only by later writers, or told different ways, this path will say so out loud. And the people will be people: brave, frightened, generous, sometimes wrong. The Qur'an calls the Messenger a good example. The people around him show what following it looked like up close: a frightened friend in a cave, being told not to grieve.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person from history you admire, famous or not: a scholar, a great-grandmother, a companion whose story you half remember, and ask what they carried that reached you, a skill, a book, a kind of courage. If you pray, you can ask Allah's mercy for them; if you don't, simply stay with them, and notice that it came this far because they carried it.
Sirah. The story of the Prophet's life ﷺ, carried through companions and the generations after, each handing it to the next. Today's word.

698.title: The peninsula
698.hook: desert, oases, trade routes, and a people who prized poetry and hospitality
698.carry: a land of wells and words
698.howItsDone: Mosque classes and sirah books often begin the Prophet's story with the land of Arabia before Islam: Mecca's dry valley, its trade, and the customs of hospitality and poetry the Qur'an's first listeners knew.

segments.voice: Yesterday the sirah began, the long story people carried. Your line was: people carried it.

Sand ridges, for days. Then, low on the horizon, a smudge of green: date palms around a well. A line of camels turns toward it, and everyone in the caravan already knows that well's name, who holds it, and what it costs to drink there. This is where the sirah starts. Before a single verse came down, before the Prophet ﷺ was born, there was this land of distances, water and words.
screen: `SAND, FOR DAYS.` → `A SMUDGE OF GREEN.` → `WHERE THE STORY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Arabic calls the place jazirat al-'arab, the island of the Arabs, since the word jazirah can mean island or peninsula. The Qur'an speaks to people who knew this land in their bodies. When Ibrahim leaves his family near the House, his prayer in surah fourteen calls the place, in Pickthall's words, "an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House." No crops. Tradition places Mecca in that valley. So how did people live there? Trade. Surah one hundred six, named for the tribe of Quraysh, speaks of their caravans setting out in winter and in summer, and asks them to worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear. A desert town's living, in a few short lines. Not all the land was empty, though. There were oases, with wells and palm groves, and towns grew up around them. One of them the Qur'an calls Yathrib, the town later known as Medina. Along the routes between them, tradition remembers two things held in honor. The first was hospitality. Where a traveler without water could die, taking in a guest was not a nicety. Stories are still told of Hatim of the tribe of Tayy, remembered as a byword for giving. The second was words: poems memorized and recited at fairs and around fires. A good line could make a tribe proud. A sharp one could wound. The Qur'an arrives in exactly this world. When it speaks of rain from the sky bringing dead land back to life, its first listeners knew what dead land looked like. And when it challenged them to bring a surah like it, it was speaking to listeners who knew what language could do.

699.title: The tribes
699.hook: life was held together by tribe and clan, for protection and for honor
699.howItsDone: Qur'an 49:13 is recited in sermons and classes on family, race and belonging, and the hadith about helping an oppressor by stopping him is taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peninsula. Your line was: a land of wells and words.

Who are your people? In Mecca before Islam, the answer could decide whether you lived. Ask a man his name and he would give you a chain: son of this one, of that clan, of that tribe. There was no police force and no state. Your clan was your protection. Harm one of its members and the whole clan answered. Lose your clan and you stood alone in the open. Today's word is the thing that held that world together.
screen: `WHO ARE YOUR PEOPLE?` → `NO POLICE, NO STATE.` → `YOUR CLAN WAS YOUR SHIELD.`

segments.voice: The word is qabilah: a tribe. As the sirah describes it, a tribe was made of clans, and clans of families, nested like rooms in a house. In Mecca the tribe was Quraysh, and among its clans was Banu Hashim, the clan the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would be born into. Belonging gave you honor, a name to stand behind, and above all protection. The custom of blood vengeance meant an attack on one person was an attack on the clan. That threat kept people safe. It also kept feuds burning. The protective side matters later: the sirah tells how the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib, of the same clan, sheltered him when others turned hostile. But tribal loyalty could also mean standing by your own, right or wrong. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says: help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. The companions were puzzled. Helping the oppressed, yes. But how do you help an oppressor? By stopping him from oppressing, he answered. Some readers hear in the first half an echo of an old desert saying, turned inside out by the second. Loyalty stays. Its job changes. Surah forty-nine uses this very word, in the plural. Pickthall translates: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Tribes are not erased. They are given a purpose. And the verse goes on, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." In a world that measured honor by lineage, that turned the ladder sideways. Your line still names you. It no longer ranks you.

700.title: Poets at the fair
700.hook: at the fairs of 'Ukaz poets competed, and the best odes were honored
700.howItsDone: Classical Arabic poetry from before Islam is still studied by Muslims and students of Arabic, partly to understand the language the Qur'an's first listeners knew; the Qur'an itself is recited, not sung as poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qabilah, the tribe. Your line was: belonging protected you.

Dust, tents, the smell of leather and spice. Traders have come from across the peninsula to a market called 'Ukaz. But one crowd isn't gathered around the goods. It's gathered around a man standing up to speak. A long poem comes out, measured and rhymed, line after line landing on the same sound. When he finishes, people repeat his best lines to each other. By the time the caravans leave, those lines will travel farther than any bale of cloth. Today: poets at the fair.
screen: `A MARKET CALLED 'UKAZ.` → `A CROWD AROUND A SPEAKER.` → `LINES THAT TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Ibn Abbas, a young cousin of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, names 'Ukaz in Sahih al-Bukhari as one of the markets of the days before Islam. Later writers remember it as a place where poets performed and were judged. The Arabic word for poet is sha'ir. Poems that come down from that time praised a tribe's courage, mourned the dead, described a camel, or lingered over an abandoned campsite where a beloved once lived. Tradition says a great poem could make a tribe famous, and a mocking one could shame it. Later writers gathered a set of odes called the Mu'allaqat, the hung ones, and a story people tell says they were hung on the Ka'ba. That story is disputed, and the name's first meaning is uncertain. So when the Qur'an came, it came to listeners who knew good language the way some people know good bread. Some in Mecca called the Prophet a poet; surah fifty-two quotes them saying so. The Qur'an answers directly. Surah thirty-six says Allah did not teach him poetry, and that it does not befit him. Surah sixty-nine says this is not the speech of a poet. That isn't the Qur'an calling poetry worthless. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says that some poetry is wisdom. It is the Qur'an saying: this is something else. And the people best placed to hear the difference were the ones who had stood in the crowd at 'Ukaz, and knew exactly what a poem sounded like.
screen: `'UKAZ: A MARKET BEFORE ISLAM.` · `SHA'IR: POET.` · `THE HUNG ODES, AND A DISPUTED STORY.` · `NOT THE SPEECH OF A POET.` · then, large: `SOME POETRY IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Find one line you love, a verse a grandparent used to quote, a lyric, a few words of the Qur'an if you know them, and say it aloud slowly, then once more, softer, listening for where it rises and which word carries the weight. Then sit in the quiet after it. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the gift of speech; if you don't, simply notice what a few words just did to the room.
